## Before you start clicking through {.smaller}

This deck is an **overview**, not the material. The four written parts have
the details: worked examples, the exceptions, what breaks and why:

- [Part 1 — The command line](parts/01-command-line.qmd)
- [Part 2 — Installing and managing tools](parts/02-packages.qmd)
- [Part 3 — Git and GitHub](parts/03-git.qmd)
- [Part 4 — Files you will meet](parts/04-file-formats.qmd)

**You need only Part 1 before a first practical.** If you have little time,
read Part 1 carefully, and use the rest of this deck as a preview.

::: {.notes}
If presenting live: say this out loud before moving on. The deck is
deliberately thin — if a question digs into detail, that is what the
corresponding part is for, not a reason to improvise an answer here.
:::

## Why a terminal at all?

A fair question, before you spend an evening on this.

- **Many tools exist only there.** Most scientific software has no graphical
  interface. Another program can run a command-line program a thousand times.
  It cannot run a program that needs a person to click.
- **It is a record.** You can copy a command into a methods section, run it
  again next year, and someone else can check it. You cannot do this with
  clicks.
- **It works the same for many files.** The command for one file also works
  for four hundred files, without changes.

The disadvantage: a terminal does not show what it can do. It shows a cursor
and waits. Part 1 teaches you what to type.

# Part 1 — The command line

## Reading the prompt

![Own figure.](figures/prompt-anatomy.svg){fig-alt="A terminal prompt: user1 at machine, colon, tilde slash projects, dollar sign, block cursor. A key identifies user1 as the username, machine as the computer, the path as where you are, and the dollar sign as the shell being ready."}

The most important part is **where you are now**. It changes as you move
around, and it answers the question that confuses beginners most often.

## The filesystem is one tree

![Own figure.](figures/filesystem-tree.svg){fig-alt="A tree diagram rooted at a single forward slash, branching into home, bin and etc. home branches into user directories; one user directory branches into Documents, Downloads and files."}

There are no drive letters. Everything — a second disk, a USB stick, a network
drive — is a directory *somewhere inside this one tree*. And names are
**case-sensitive**: `Data.csv` and `data.csv` are two different files.

## Moving around

```bash
mkdir -p demo && cd demo
pwd
echo "hello" > notes.txt
ls -l
```

```text
/home/user1/demo
-rw-r--r-- 1 user1 staff 6 Sep 26 07:08 notes.txt
```

`pwd`, `ls` and `cd` answer *where am I?* and *what is here?* Ask these two
questions before you do anything else.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Press Tab. Every time, not only when you are stuck.

A file name typed from memory is a guess. A name that the shell completed is
not: either it is spelled correctly, or the file does not exist. We repeat this
because people forget it most often when they are in a hurry.
:::

## Parameters change what a command does

```bash
printf "alpha,12\nbeta,7\ngamma,103\n" > scores.csv
sort -t, -k2 -n -r scores.csv
```

```text
gamma,103
alpha,12
beta,7
```

Four parameters, four jobs: `-t,` the separator, `-k2` which column, `-n`
compare as numbers, `-r` largest first. Without `-n`, `103` comes *before*
`12`, because as text it starts with a smaller character.

## Never put a space in a name you create

The shell splits what you type at each space. So it cannot tell a space
inside a file name from a space between two arguments.

```text
cd lab notebook
bash: cd: lab: No such file or directory
```

`cd` received **two** arguments, not one. Quotes (`cd "lab notebook"`) fix
it, but the real fix is simpler: use `lab_notebook`, and the problem never
occurs. Graphical file managers and Windows allow spaces in names, so you meet
this problem for the first time in the terminal.

## Pipes: small tools, chained

```bash
printf "banana\napple\ncherry\napple\n" | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
```

```text
      2 apple
      1 cherry
      1 banana
```

Read it from left to right, as a sentence: sort, count the repeated lines,
then sort *that result* as numbers. None of these four tools knows about the
others. With the pipe, simple tools answer a question that no single program
was written for.

## Wildcards, briefly

```bash
mkdir -p logs && touch logs/a.log logs/b.log logs/notes.txt
ls logs/*.log
```

```text
logs/a.log
logs/b.log
```

`*` matches any number of characters. Before you use it with `rm`, check with
`ls` which files it matches.

## Part 1, in one line

Terminal, tree, parameters, pipes, wildcards. **[The full page →](parts/01-command-line.qmd)**
also covers the backslash at the end of a line, `stdin`/`stdout`/`stderr`, how
to read error messages, a short section on variables such as `$HOME`, and a

# Part 2 — Installing and managing tools

## The problem environments solve

Two projects can need **different versions of the same dependency**, and the
versions may not work together. An **environment** stops the tools of one
project from breaking the tools of another. If the environment is written down
in a file, someone else can rebuild it and get the same result.

```{.bash .no-run}
pixi init myproject && cd myproject
pixi add python samtools
pixi run python --version
```

You do not need to "activate" anything. `pixi run` uses the tools of this
project because you are in the directory of this project.

::: {.notes}
Not executed: installing needs the network and takes minutes. The full page
runs through this properly, plus the conda/mamba translation table for when
someone hands you instructions written the old way.
:::

## Part 2, in one line

`pixi.toml` says what you asked for, and `pixi.lock` says exactly what you got.
Commit both files. **[The full page →](parts/02-packages.qmd)** also covers
conda and mamba. You will see both in documentation, even if you never install
them.

# Part 3 — Git and GitHub

## Four stages, one command between each

![Own figure.](figures/git-stages.svg){fig-alt="Four boxes: Workspace, Staging area, Local repository, Remote repository. Workspace to Staging area via git add, Staging area to Local repository via git commit, Local repository to Remote repository via git push. A dashed arrow labelled git pull or git clone runs back from Remote repository to Workspace."}

```bash
git config --global user.name "You"          # one-time, per machine
git config --global user.email "you@example.org"

mkdir -p repo && cd repo && git init -q
echo "print('hello')" > analysis.py
git add analysis.py
git commit -q -m "Add the analysis script"
git log --oneline
```

```text
9c1f2ab Add the analysis script
```

## Branches, and the error you will actually see

If a team shares one repository, this happens in the first hour:

```text
 ! [rejected]        main -> main (fetch first)
```

Nothing is lost. Git refuses to overwrite someone else's work with yours. The
fix, and a good habit from the start: work on a **branch**, push it, and open a
**pull request**, so that someone reads your changes before they go into
`main`.

::: {.notes}
The GitHub side (pushing a branch, the Compare & pull request button) is
prose on the full page, not a command — it is an interactive web UI and the
exact buttons move, so it is described as "what to look for," not a fixed
click path.
:::

## Take care of your GitHub profile

**You will need an account.** At least one person per team needs one, so that
the shared repository can exist. In practice everyone needs one, because each
of you pushes your own commits.

See it as more than a requirement. With pinned repositories, a short
biography and a clear README for each project, your profile becomes a
portfolio. One real example:
**[github.com/jonas-fuchs](https://github.com/jonas-fuchs)**.

When you apply for a job in this field, your profile can say more than a CV. It
shows that you can do the work, instead of only claiming it.

::: {.notes}
If presenting live, slow down here. Students benefit from hearing this early;
it is not a footnote. The profile does not need to be finished this semester,
but it needs to *start*.
:::

## Part 3, in one line

`add` → `commit` → `push`. If other people share the repository, create a
branch before you push. **[The full page →](parts/03-git.qmd)** covers diff,
restore, merge conflicts, and every step from a branch to a pull request.

# Part 4 — Files you will meet

## Two formats you cannot avoid

```bash
cat > README.md <<'EOF'
# My project
A short description, a `code` span, and a [link](notes.md).
EOF

python3 -c "
import json
d = {'sample': 'A1', 'passed': True, 'count': 1420}
print(json.dumps(d))
"
```

```text
{"sample": "A1", "passed": true, "count": 1420}
```

READMEs and GitHub pages are written in **Markdown**. Tools use **JSON** to
pass structured results to each other: six data types, no comments, no comma
after the last item.

# Before your first practical

## Getting a terminal, easiest first {.smaller}

Reading the commands is not the same as running them. So first you need a place
to type them. Any of these works.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Nothing to install** | [webvm.io](https://webvm.io) starts a real Debian Linux in a browser tab. No account, no download. Enough for all of Part 1. |
| **On a Mac** | You already have one: *Applications → Utilities → Terminal*. |
| **On Windows** | Install **WSL2**: run `wsl --install` in PowerShell as administrator, then restart. It is a real Ubuntu, and everything here then works for you without changes. |
| **The long-term way** | Install Linux on your own computer. Nothing here needs it, but everything here is easier with it. |

The browser version forgets everything when you close the tab, and you cannot
install software in it. So from Part 2 on, you need one of the other three.

::: {.notes}
The point of the table is that nobody is blocked. The most common reason why
someone arrives having read nothing is that step one was an installation they
had no time for. The first row removes that reason.

WSL2 is still the right answer for a Windows user who will do this more than
once: it is a real Ubuntu, and the alternative is software that has no Windows
build at all.

Say this out loud: some courses give you a prepared machine, and if yours
does, you do not need any of this.
:::

## What to do this week

- **Get a terminal**, in the easiest of the ways above.
- Work through **[Part 1](parts/01-command-line.qmd)** carefully. *Type* the
  commands, and check yourself against the list at the end.
- Install **[VS Code](https://code.visualstudio.com)**, and on Windows its
  **WSL** extension.
- Come back to Parts 2–4 when you need them. Nobody expects you to know them
  in advance.

If your course gives you a prepared machine, you do not need to set anything
up. But an hour of typing in a terminal of your own still helps: afterwards,
the prepared machine feels familiar and not mysterious.

::: {.notes}
If presenting live, this is the slide to slow down on — it is the one with an
action attached, unlike everything before it.

The last paragraph is the one to say in your own words. A reader who has only
ever been handed a working machine has no model of what it is doing, and that
